name: Credential Stuffing and Multi-Factor Authentication
intent: Defend logins against attackers who replay passwords leaked from other sites: know which limits miss the attack, add a second factor that matches the threat, and do not leave account recovery as the back door.
scenario: A shop has 2,000 customer accounts. A list of 20,000 email and password pairs from an unrelated breach is replayed against its login page, one try per pair, from thousands of addresses.
problem: People reuse passwords, so a leak at one site becomes a key to many others. Credential stuffing is not guessing: each try uses a password that was once correct for that person, so the attacker gets in with one attempt per account, spread across many addresses so no single address or account looks busy. The classic defences, limits per account and per address, were designed for guessing and barely see it.

howItWorks.title: What the attack looks like
howItWorks.text: The attacker has pairs from an old leak and replays them, usually with automation and a large pool of addresses such as a botnet or rented proxies. Most tries fail because the email does not exist here or the password changed. The few that match, commonly reported as somewhere between a fraction of a percent and a couple of percent of tries, are real takeovers, and the attacker never trips an account lockout because each account is tried once.

howItWorks.title: Limits: per account, per address, per credential
howItWorks.text: A per-account limit stops one account being hammered, but not one try on each of many accounts. A per-address limit stops a single machine, but not thousands of addresses each trying a few times. Limiting by the credential, for example checking the submitted password against lists of known-breached passwords, or by a device and behaviour signal, looks at what is being tried rather than who is trying it. Rate limits still matter as a cost on the attacker, and are not enough on their own.

howItWorks.title: Add a second factor that matches the threat
howItWorks.text: With a second factor, a correct leaked password alone is not enough. An SMS code can be intercepted or redirected by taking over a phone number and can be relayed through a fake login page. An authenticator app code (TOTP) is not sent over the phone network, but a fake page can still ask for it and pass it on in real time. A push prompt that only asks to tap approve is open to fatigue: the attacker triggers prompts until a tired user taps yes. Number matching, where the user types a number shown on the login screen, defeats blind approval, but a live phishing page can still show the victim the right number, so it does not stop a relay. A passkey signs a challenge that the browser binds to the real site's domain, so a fake page on another domain gets nothing usable and there is no code to read out.

howItWorks.title: Close the back door: account recovery
howItWorks.text: Every route that can reset or bypass the second factor is as strong as the factor itself. If a link sent to an email address resets the password and skips the second factor, an attacker who can read that mailbox, perhaps with the same reused password, wins. Make recovery require something comparable, such as a recovery code stored when the factor was set up, a waiting period with notices to every channel, and a second factor on the mailbox itself.

howItWorks.title: Layer and measure
howItWorks.text: Combine: breached-password checks at sign-up and login, a second factor offered to all and required for sensitive accounts, rate limits as a cost, bot detection, alerts to users about new-device logins, and strong recovery. Watch the failed-login ratio, the share of accounts with a second factor, and recovery requests, because a spike in any of them is the first sign of an attack.

pros: A second factor makes a reused password useless on its own, the root cause of this attack
Breached-password checks catch known-leaked passwords however many addresses the attack comes from
Passkeys remove both the password to leak and the code to phish
Each layer is cheap compared with the cost of a wave of account takeovers
cons: Second factors add friction, and a share of users will not enrol unless it is required
SMS and plain push are weaker than they look, and stronger options cost more to roll out
Account recovery is hard to make both safe and friendly to people who lose their phone
Lockout rules can be abused to lock real users out of their own accounts
whenToUse: Any login with accounts worth taking: payments, stored cards, personal data, loyalty points
Right after seeing a spike of failed logins from many addresses, or a breach elsewhere that involves your users
Offer a second factor to everyone, and require it for staff, admins and high-value accounts
whenNotToUse: Do not treat a per-IP or per-account rate limit as the defence against this attack: it is a cost, not a stop
Do not lock accounts after a few failures as the only answer: attackers can use it to lock victims out
pitfalls: Relying on per-IP and per-account limits: a botnet makes a few tries per address and one try per account, so neither limit fires
Assuming any second factor is the same: SMS can be intercepted, TOTP and number-matched push can be relayed through a fake page, and tap-to-approve push can be worn down
Push approvals without number matching or a limit on prompts, which invites fatigue attacks (repeated prompts at night until someone taps yes)
Recovery by email link that skips the second factor, so the second factor protects only the front door
Offering a second factor but not requiring it for admins, so the highest-value accounts are the ones left open
Locking accounts after a few failures, which lets an attacker lock real users out on purpose
Checking passwords against breach lists only at sign-up, not at login, when new leaks appear later
Different error messages for unknown account and wrong password, which tells the attacker which emails exist

quiz.question: A login allows 5 failed attempts per account per hour and 20 per IP address per hour. An attacker replays one leaked password for each of 2,000 accounts from 5,000 addresses, and many accounts are taken over. Why did the limits not fire?
options: The limits were set too high, and 3 per account would have stopped it
Each account got one try and each address got a few, so no counter reached its limit
Rate limits only work against attackers who use real browsers
The attacker bypassed the limits by using HTTPS
quiz.explanation: Stuffing is spread out: one try per account and a handful per address. Counters keyed on account or address never fill up. Lowering the limits would only start to lock out real users, and the transport protocol is irrelevant to counting.

quiz.question: A company adds push approval for logins: users get a prompt and tap Approve. Attackers with leaked passwords start triggering prompts at 3 a.m., and some users approve to make them stop. Which change addresses this best?
options: Send the prompts more often, so that users notice the pattern sooner
Make the Approve button smaller to reduce accidental taps
Replace push with a code sent by SMS, which cannot be approved by accident
Require number matching, where the user types the number shown on the login screen, and cap the prompts per account
quiz.explanation: Number matching means a blind tap is not enough, because the number appears only where the real login is happening. Capping prompts limits the pressure. More prompts make fatigue worse, button size does not matter, and SMS codes have weaknesses of their own.

quiz.question: A site requires a passkey for every user, yet attackers still take over accounts. The reset flow sends a link to the registered email address, and that link skips the passkey. What is the lesson?
options: Recovery is part of the login, so it must be as strong as the second factor it can bypass
Passkeys are weak and should be replaced by SMS codes
Email links should be sent twice so that the owner is more likely to see them
Users should be forced to pick longer passwords, which fixes recovery
quiz.explanation: An attacker takes the weakest path. If email alone resets everything, the passkey protects only the front door. Recovery needs a comparable factor, a delay and notifications. Passkeys are not the weak part, and sending the link twice or lengthening passwords does not touch the bypass.
